beats.purpose: Pose the core question of how a passive receiver determines its exact coordinate purely by listening to radio signals from space.
beats.visual_intent: A smartphone on the ground receiving faint radio waves from overhead satellites without broadcasting any signal back.

beats.purpose: Introduce the fundamental mechanism: calculating distance from the travel time of timestamped atomic broadcasts to create intersecting range spheres.
beats.visual_intent: Expanding spherical range shells radiating from orbital satellites at the speed of light, intersecting on the surface of the Earth.

beats.purpose: Reveal that while three spheres geometrically intersect at two points, receiver clocks lack atomic synchronization, making exact transit times uncertain.
beats.visual_intent: A close-up diagram contrasting the satellite's atomic clock tick with a drift-prone receiver quartz oscillator, blurring the intersecting range surfaces.

beats.purpose: Demonstrate how introducing a fourth satellite creates a system of equations that solves for the three spatial dimensions and receiver clock bias simultaneously.
beats.visual_intent: A fourth expanding shell snapping the blurred intersection into one precise spatial coordinate and aligning receiver time.

beats.purpose: Summarize how continuous multi-satellite time-of-flight measurements provide seamless, instant positioning anywhere on Earth.
beats.visual_intent: A dynamic orbital constellation maintaining continuous lines of sight to a user traveling across the rotating planet.

output.rationale: The subject addresses a familiar everyday marvel ('How does GPS know where I am?'). Starting with this intuitive question, establishing the basic geometric model of sphere intersection, complicating it with clock synchronization errors, and resolving it with the fourth satellite delivers the cleanest explanation.
output.title: How GPS Pinpoints You with Pure Timing
